questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}$ at the point $(1,2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =2xy+{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =3(1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+2(1)(2)=11 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =2(1)(2)+{1}^{2}-3(2)^{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-1) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z+1 & =11(x-1)-7(y-2) \\ z+1 & =11x-7y+3 \\ -11x+7y+z-2 & =0 \\ 11x-7y-z+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,4,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\sqrt{y}-\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\sqrt{y}-y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{y}}-\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4) & =\sqrt{4}-\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1}}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}-\sqrt{1}=-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-2) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,4)+(y-4)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,4) \\ z+2 & =0(x-1)-\frac{3}{4}(y-4) \\ z+2 & =-\frac{3}{4}y+3 \\ \frac{3}{4}y+z-1 & =0 \\ 3y+4z-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-x{y}^{2}) \\  & =-{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-x{y}^{2}) \\  & =1-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1) & =-{1}^{2}=-1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1) & =1-2(-1)(1)=3\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)$ at the point $(0,0,3,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,3):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0,3) & =\frac{2(0)(3)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0,3) & =\frac{2(0)(3)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(0,0,3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0,3)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0,3)+(z-3)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(0,0,3) \\ w & =0x+0y+0(z-3) \\ w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z}$ at the point $(1,1,1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})={e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x}+{e}^{y}-{e}^{z})=-{e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1}=e \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1}=e \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-{e}^{1}=-e\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-e & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w-e & =e(x-1)+e(y-1)-e(z-1) \\ w-e & =ex-e+ey-e-ez+e \\ -ex-ey+ez+w & =0 \\ ex+ey-ez-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,1,1,0).$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz)$ at the point $(-1,1,1,-\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx}$ at the point $(2,2,2,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{z}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-6 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) \\ w-6 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+(z-2) \\ w-6 & =x+y+z-6 \\ -x-y-z+w & =0 \\ x+y+z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
At which points on the surface $z=4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6$  is the tangent plane 
horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =8xy+{y}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨8xy+{y}^{3},\,4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}8xy+{y}^{3}=0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=0$ or ${y}^{2}+8x=0.$ So, we have two cases.

- If $y=0$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(0)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

- If ${y}^{2}=-8x$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(-8x)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Substituting $x=0$ back into ${y}^{2}=-8x$ gives

$$
{y}^{2}=-8(0)\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

So, in both cases, we have $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Finally, substituting these values into our function, we get

$$
z=4(0)^{2}(0)+(0)(0)^{3}-6=-6.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,-6).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3{x}^{2}-3,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3=0 \\ 2y+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=\pm 1$ while the second equation gives $y=-1.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=1.
$$

Substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(1)^{3}-3(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=-3.
$$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-3).$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2x+2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-4,0,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x+2,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩=⟨-4,0,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}c(2x+2)=-4 \\ c(2y+2)=0 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-(2x+2)=-4\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-(2y+2)=0\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(1)^{2}+2(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(1,-1,2).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨3,5,-1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3x-\frac{1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨3,5,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩=⟨3,5,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3cy=3 \\ 3cx-\frac{c}{y}=5 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3(1)y=3\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
3(1)x-\frac{1}{1}=5\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\  & =3(2)(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(2,1,6).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0 \\ \frac{2y}{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2})=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z= x^2 + xy$ at the point $(1,2, 3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2x+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =2(1)+2=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-3 & =4(x-1)+1(y-2) \\ z-3 & =4x+y-6 \\ -4x-y+z+3 & =0 \\ 4x+y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xyz$ at the point $(1,-1,1,5).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2x-2yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2y-2xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2z-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(-1)(1)=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =2(-1)-2(1)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(1)(-1)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =4(x-1)-4(y+1)+4(z-1) \\ w-5 & =4x-4y+4z-12 \\ -4x+4y-4z+w+7 & =0 \\ 4x-4y+4z-w-7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: At which points on the surface $z={y^2}+ {xy}$  is the tangent plane horizontal?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108364/assets/df6542baabd72b24ce115cb79c912c7b19fd3bd1b663467956445553b60a68c1.png) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$
